body:
- **Spread and flow capture:** Retail in India buys cheap, short-dated OTM options, and 70% of turnover was 0DTE in FY25. Market makers who sell them collect:
  - the spread;
  - the implied-over-realised volatility premium;
  - the "lottery premium" on far-OTM strikes.
  Because about 700 professional algo entities quote against millions of manual traders, adverse selection runs against retail. Professionals reprice faster than retail can react.
- **Information and risk systems:** Firms see the whole order book across cash, futures and options. They hedge delta in milliseconds and net exposures across thousands of instruments. Retail holds unhedged directional bets.
- **Cost:** Exchange co-location, member-level fees and no brokerage give professionals a per-trade cost a fraction of retail's. Retail costs total about ₹25,000 crore a year.
- **Capital:** Balance sheet size lets a firm warehouse risk and survive tail days. In the Jane Street allegation it also let the firm move the underlying.

`case_study:enphase-2016-2025` · tickers US-ENPH · confidence: single-source

Microinverter maker trading below ~$1 in 2016-17 with going-concern-type worries [unverified]. Badri Kothandaraman (COO 2017, CEO Sept 2017) ran a cost/pricing/opex plan: redesigned IQ microinverters, cut costs, raised prices, refinanced debt; gross margin from ~20% to ~40%+ [unverified]. Joined S&P 500 Jan 2021. Peak ~$340 (Dec 2022) [unverified] ≈ 400x from the low. Split: loss-to-profit plus P/E up to ~100x; US residential solar boom (30% 25D tax credit, IRA 2022), California NEM 2.0. Bust: California NEM 3.0 (Apr 2023) cut payback economics, rates rose (solar loans), European distributor inventory glut 2023-24, SolarEdge-style channel destock; then the July 2025 tax law phased out the 25D credit for customer-owned systems after 2025. Stock $40.47 mid-2025 (-67% from Aug 2024's $123.65), ~$30s late 2025: ~-90% from peak [unverified]. EARLY SIGNAL (up) visible 2018: gross margin rising quarter after quarter with a new CEO's public 3-step plan, while the stock was <$5. EARLY SIGNAL (down): demand dependent on one state's net-metering rule and federal credits, plus distributor inventory rising faster than installs. Who caught it: few documented; retail/momentum. LESSON: a genuine operational turnaround can ride a policy-subsidised boom to 400x, but demand that exists because of subsidies reverses when policy and rates turn; treat as cyclical, not compounder.

- **Start → end:** <$1 (2016-17) [unverified] → ~$340 peak (Dec 2022) [unverified]; ~$30-40 (2025) (~400x up, ~-90% down)
- **EPS vs rerating:** loss-to-profit + P/E to ~100x
- **Max drawdown:** ~-90% (Dec 2022-2025)
- **Early signal:** up: GM expansion under new CEO; down: NEM 3.0, rates, channel inventory, 25D phase-out
- **Who caught it:** not documented
- **Ended/stalled:** Dec 2022 peak
- **Lesson:** subsidy-driven demand is cyclical; policy is the hidden variable

`strategy:bakshi-bad-news-moats` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, process, quality, behavior

As taught in Bakshi's public lectures and blog: (1) Identify businesses with durable moats - pricing power, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, brands, regulatory licences - evidenced by stable high ROCE. (2) Wait for 'bad news' that is temporary or non-structural: a regulatory scare, a one-off loss, an industry panic, a management change misread by the market. (3) Separate temporary from permanent: does the bad news damage the moat, or only this year's earnings? (4) Use behavioural finance to exploit overreaction (loss aversion, recency bias) and to check one's own biases. (5) Prefer 'clean surprises': hidden strengths that later show up in reported numbers. Indian examples of the pattern (not his holdings): high-quality lenders after one-off asset-quality scares, consumer franchises during temporary input-cost spikes. Risk: misjudging a permanent moat break (technology disruption, regulation) as temporary.

Links: person:sanjay-bakshi (about); strategy:buffett-munger (similar_to)

Sources: <https://www.safalniveshak.com/fundoo-professor-sanjay-bakshi/> ; <https://www.safalniveshak.com/one-percent-show-prof-sanjay-bakshi-transcript/>

body:
`insight:buffett-volatility-not-risk-2014` | confidence: verified | date: 2015-02-27

2014 (50th-anniversary) letter: business schools use volatility as a proxy for risk; 'this pedagogic assumption makes for easy teaching, it is dead wrong: Volatility is far from synonymous with risk.' The real risk is loss of purchasing power over the holding period. Caveat stated plainly: 'owning equities for a day or a week or a year is far riskier ... than leaving funds in cash-equivalents', relevant to anyone 'forced to sell securities during depressed markets', and 'any party that might have meaningful near-term needs for funds should keep appropriate sums in Treasuries or insured bank deposits.' For multi-decade investors, 'a diversified equity portfolio, bought over time, will prove far less risky than dollar-based securities.' 2024 letter adds the currency angle: 'Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails ... Fixed-coupon bonds provide no protection against runaway currency', and Berkshire 'will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses.' 2008: the 'U.S. Treasury bond bubble of late 2008' - 'Clinging to cash equivalents ... is almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long.' Actionable for an Indian investor: segregate a 2-3 year cash/FD/liquid-fund need bucket so no equity sale is ever forced; above that, measure risk as permanent loss and real (INR-inflation-adjusted) return, not drawdown size.

Sources:
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2014ltr.pdf
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2024ltr.pdf
- https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/2008ltr.pdf

- `shares` must use the same scale as the money units: ₹ cr goes with shares in crore, $M with shares in millions.
- `net_debt` is negative for net cash. Leave out lease liabilities when rent sits inside the margin you use (Indian pre-Ind AS 116 EBITDA; US retailers with occupancy in COGS).
- Use the **economic** margin: pre-Ind AS 116 for Indian retailers, core (ex other income) for cash-rich companies, and after SBC.
